description: Hey everyone! I'm a Computer Science student at SNHU, focusing on Software Engineering. I've always loved technology, whether it's coding, fixing electronics, or figuring out how things work. I have experience with Python, SQL, and building games and applications. My dream is to become a software engineer at NASA! This is my first Space Apps Challenge, so I'm excited and a little nervous! I'm planning to work solo, but I'd love to connect with others and learn along the way!
summary:
ASTERIA is an interactive web application I developed to explore some of the challenges involved in planning lunar missions, particularly near the Moon's south pole. One of the biggest challenges in this region is understanding how sunlight and Earth's position can affect landing conditions, power availability, and communication opportunities. I wanted to create something that would make this information easier to explore without requiring users to navigate complicated scientific tools.

Through ASTERIA, users can explore four potential lunar landing regions, adjust dates and times, and view interactive graphs showing simulated Sun and Earth elevations. I also included a comparison system that allows users to evaluate different locations based on mission priorities, such as solar power and communication visibility.

Although ASTERIA is currently a prototype that uses simulated data rather than verified lunar measurements, my goal was to demonstrate how thoughtful software design could make complex aerospace concepts more understandable and accessible. I believe tools like this have the potential to support both future mission-planning applications and STEM education.
details:
ASTERIA began with a question: How can we make the challenges of landing near the Moon's south pole easier to understand and explore?

Unlike many locations on Earth, the lunar south pole presents unusual lighting conditions, and communication with Earth is not always straightforward. These factors matter when considering where future missions might operate, especially when solar power and direct communication are important.

I developed ASTERIA as an interactive web-based prototype that brings these considerations into one dashboard. Users can explore four lunar regions, adjust dates and times, and view visual representations of the Sun's and Earth's positions relative to the horizon. The application also includes a comparison system that lets users prioritize sunlight, communication, or a balance of both. An export feature allows users to save the results of their exploration.

The application was built using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with interactive charts and a responsive interface. I focused on creating a design that feels like a professional mission-control system while remaining approachable for students, educators, and people who may not have experience with aerospace software.

One important limitation is that the current version uses simulated calculations and illustrative site scores. It does not yet incorporate validated lunar ephemeris, local terrain horizons, or actual communication predictions. I chose to make this distinction clear because scientific accuracy is essential in aerospace applications.

My next goal would be to integrate authoritative NASA data and more advanced modeling so that ASTERIA could move beyond a conceptual demonstration. For now, it shows how software engineering and thoughtful interface design can make complicated space exploration concepts easier to investigate.
